function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.content:
**Java** is a high‑level, class‑based, object‑oriented programming language that was originally developed by James Gosling and his team at Sun Microsystems (now owned by Oracle Corporation). It was first released in 1995 as part of the Sun Microsystems Java platform.

---

## 1. Core Characteristics

| Feature | What it means |
|---------|---------------|
| **Platform‑independent** | Code is compiled into *bytecode* that runs on the Java Virtual Machine (JVM). The same bytecode works on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, etc. |
| **Object‑oriented** | Everything is an object (except primitives). Supports encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, and abstraction. |
| **Strongly typed** | Variables must be declared with a type; type checking happens at compile time. |
| **Automatic memory management** | Garbage collector frees unused objects, reducing memory leaks. |
| **Rich standard library** | Includes collections, I/O, networking, concurrency, GUI (Swing, JavaFX), database access (JDBC), and more. |
| **Security** | JVM sandbox, bytecode verification, and security manager help protect against malicious code. |
| **Multithreading** | Built‑in support for concurrent execution via `Thread`, `Runnable`, `ExecutorService`, etc. |

---

## 2. Typical Use Cases

| Domain | Why Java is popular |
|--------|---------------------|
| **Enterprise applications** | Robust, scalable, and supported by frameworks like Spring, Jakarta EE, and Hibernate. |
| **Android apps** | Android’s native language (until Kotlin became the preferred choice). |
| **Web servers & microservices** | High performance, strong typing, and mature ecosystem (Spring Boot, Micronaut). |
| **Big data & analytics** | Hadoop, Spark, Flink, and other big‑data tools are written in Java or provide Java APIs. |
| **Embedded systems** | Java ME (Micro Edition) and Java SE Embedded for IoT devices. |
| **Desktop GUIs** | Swing, JavaFX, and third‑party libraries for cross‑platform desktop apps. |

---

## 3. How Java Works (The Compile‑Run Cycle)

1. **Source code (`.java`)** – Human‑readable text.
2. **Compilation (`javac`)** – Translates source into bytecode (`.class` files).
3. **Bytecode verification** – JVM checks for safety and correctness.
4. **Execution (`java`)** – JVM interprets or just‑in‑time compiles bytecode into native machine code.

Because the bytecode is platform‑agnostic, you can compile once and run anywhere that has a compatible JVM.

---

## 4. Common Java Syntax (Hello World)

```java
public class HelloWorld {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello, world!");
    }
}
```

Compile: `javac HelloWorld.java`  
Run: `java HelloWorld`

---

## 5. Java vs. JavaScript (Quick Clarification)

| Aspect | Java | JavaScript |
|--------|------|------------|
| Origin | 1995, Sun Microsystems | 1995, Netscape |
| Paradigm | Object‑oriented, strongly typed | Prototype‑based, loosely typed |
| Runtime | JVM (desktop, server, Android) | Browser, Node.js |
| Use | Enterprise, Android, server, desktop | Web front‑end, server (Node.js) |

Despite the similar name, they are unrelated languages.

---

## 6. Popular Java Ecosystem

| Category | Examples |
|----------|----------|
| **Build tools** | Maven, Gradle, Ant |
| **Testing** | JUnit, TestNG, Mockito |
| **Dependency injection** | Spring Framework, CDI |
| **ORM** | Hibernate, MyBatis |
| **Web frameworks** | Spring MVC, Jakarta EE, Micronaut |
| **Reactive** | Project Reactor, RxJava |
| **IDE** | IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse, NetBeans |

---

## 7. Learning Resources

| Resource | Type | Link |
|----------|------|------|
| Official Java Tutorials | Documentation | https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/ |
| “Effective Java” (Joshua Bloch) | Book | https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/effective-java-3rd/9780134686097/ |
| Java Programming and Software Engineering Fundamentals (Coursera) | Course | https://www.coursera.org/specializations/java-programming |
| JetBrains Academy – Java track | Interactive | https://www.jetbrains.com/academy/ |
| LeetCode – Java problems | Practice | https://leetcode.com/problemset/all/?language=Java |

---

### TL;DR

Java is a versatile, mature programming language designed for portability, reliability, and scalability. Its bytecode runs on the JVM, making it a go‑to choice for enterprise back‑ends, Android apps, big‑data tools, and more. Whether you’re building a web service, a desktop GUI, or an embedded system, Java’s extensive ecosystem and strong typing make it a solid foundation.
